# AI Terminal Pet bridge for DeepSeek Harness

A Host-only Cordis bundle that reports DeepSeek Harness session state to the
AI Terminal Pet desktop overlay.

## What it does

| Harness event | Overlay state |
| --- | --- |
| `turn/start`, `agent/inbox/claimed`, `agent/status` running | `working` |
| `tool/call` | `tool_use` |
| `approval/asked`, `approval/request` | `waiting_permission` |
| `tool/result` with error, `command/done` error, `agent/error` | `error` |
| `turn/end`, `command/done` success | `idle` |
| Harness process exit | `closed` |

The overlay then plays an alert tone and shows a tray balloon on those
transitions, and its one-click jump button targets the Harness window.

## Protocol source

This bundle contains **no** pipe-name, state-set or snapshot logic of its own.
It loads the official protocol module from
`%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\protocol.js`, which `scripts/install.ps1` copies from
`reporters/protocol.js` and verifies by SHA256 on every install. All reports
are fire-and-forget; a missing overlay never affects Harness.

Session id = Harness `session.header.id`; `pid` is a synthetic
`stableProcessId`, `parentPid` is the real Harness process id. Sessions are
closed explicitly on exit so the overlay does not accumulate ghosts.

## Install into DeepSeek Harness

The `desktop` profile is managed exclusively by the Electron application (the
`dsh` CLI refuses it), so install through the in-app plugin manager. In a
Harness conversation, ask:

```
Use plugin_manager with action install_bundle and target
"%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\bundles\ai-terminal-pet-bridge"
```

That string is pasted into the in-app manager, so the environment variable form is intended:
%LOCALAPPDATA% resolves per user, and a hard-coded C:\Users\<name>\... would be wrong on
every other machine. If the manager does not expand variables, substitute your own profile path.

That directory is a copy of this package, refreshed by `scripts/install.ps1`.
Installing links the local directory into the profile and applies
`cordis.patch.yml`; restart Harness if the manager reports `restart-required`.
Do not hand-edit the profile's `package.json` or `cordis.patch.yml`: the
desktop profile runs pnpm on startup and would discard manual edits.

To verify, start a Harness task and run:

```
"%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe" --json
```

A `deepseek-harness` session should appear and change state as the task runs.
`plugin_manager` with `remove_bundle` removes it.

## Files

- `index.js` — Host plugin (`apply(ctx, config)` + cleanup disposer)
- `cordis.patch.yml` — loader `insert:` row
- `locale/{en,zh}.json` — display metadata
- `icon.svg` — plugin-manager icon

# ai-terminal-pet

Stop glancing across terminal windows to track agent states. It costs one small executable with no account and no cloud.

![ai-terminal-pet](docs/assets/hero.png)

![Platform](https://img.shields.io/badge/platform-Windows-blue) ![Go](https://img.shields.io/badge/go-1.23-00ADD8) ![Version](https://img.shields.io/badge/version-0.9.0-blue)
![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-green) ![Size](https://img.shields.io/badge/size-4.17%20MiB-blue) ![Dependencies](https://img.shields.io/badge/dependencies-3-informational) ![Tests](https://img.shields.io/badge/tests-154-brightgreen)

> 🇬🇧 [English](#english)  ·  🇨🇳 [中文](#中文)

---

## English

### The problem

You run Claude Code, OpenCode, or Antigravity in multiple terminal windows at once. A background task prompts for permission to execute a tool, but you are focused in another window and never notice the prompt.

Fourteen minutes later, you switch back only to discover that your build has been sitting idle the entire time. Glancing across multiple terminal tabs wastes focus and breaks your concentration.

ai-terminal-pet anchors a 56px strip to the screen edge. It aggregates your sessions in real time, pulses when an agent needs permission, and displays which project is waiting and for how long.

The table below contrasts the everyday workflow before and after using the overlay:

| Context | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Multiple terminals | Four terminal windows open; you lose track of which window needs attention. | One 56px strip on the edge of the screen aggregates every active session. |
| Blocked build | You find out a build was blocked on a permission prompt fourteen minutes ago. | The overlay pulses immediately and shows which project is waiting and for how long. |
| Context switching | You click across tabs to check whether builds and tasks are still running. | A single glance reveals current states without touching your keyboard or mouse. |

### What it looks like

![Compact strip](docs/assets/overlay-compact.png)
*Compact strip: pulsing state orb with status glyph, session count, state word, and waiting project name.*

![Expanded list](docs/assets/overlay-expanded.png)
*Expanded list: active sessions showing per-row project name, state, source hook, and relative time.*

![Many sessions](docs/assets/overlay-expanded-many.png)
*Expanded list with many sessions: six session rows followed by the overflow line showing remaining sessions.*

![Auto-approve countdown](docs/assets/overlay-auto-approve.png)
*Auto-approve countdown: draining bar with "Allow (5s)" prompt allowing manual veto before automatic permission approval.*

---

### Features

The table below outlines the core capabilities and exact runtime parameters of the application:

| Feature | What it actually does |
|---|---|
| State aggregation | Aggregates sessions across 7 states (`idle`, `thinking`, `working`, `tool_use`, `waiting_permission`, `error`, `closed`), showing the highest-priority state across all active sessions. |
| Compact and expanded panels | Compact panel occupies 56x156 logical pixels anchored to a screen edge; clicking expands to 200 px wide, displaying 1–6 rows before adding an overflow line. |
| Whole-panel gestures | Click anywhere toggles compact and expanded views, drag anywhere moves 1:1 with the cursor, and mouse wheel adjusts zoom between 65% and 160%. |
| Edge retract | Slides mostly off-screen when docked at an edge leaving a thin sliver; hovering restores it, while waiting_permission or error states override retraction to remain visible. |
| Tray menu | Right-click tray menu toggles visibility, resets position and zoom, opens settings, switches language, toggles autostart, and configures auto-approve. |
| Settings window | Native three-tab window (General, Sound, Sessions) where every change persists immediately to `config.json` without an OK button. |
| Synthesized alert tones | Generates 44.1 kHz 16-bit mono PCM WAV tones in memory across four sound schemes (`chime`, `bell`, `soft`, `pulse`), with separate gates for waiting, error, and finish. |
| Per-session alerts | Fires Windows tray notification balloons and audio alerts on transitions into `waiting_permission`, `error`, or finish states. |
| Auto-approve and denylist | Provides a 5-second veto window on permission prompts where a tap denies and silence approves; blocks commands matching the dangerous-command denylist. |
| Jump to terminal | Walks session process ancestry and matches window titles to bring the waiting terminal window or tab to the foreground. |
| Scriptable CLI | Outputs structured session state via `ai-terminal-pet --json` by reading disk snapshots, avoiding blocking on GUI processes. |
| Single instance | A named mutex makes a second launch activate the running overlay instead of starting another one. |
| Connection capacity | The pipe server accepts 32 concurrent connections with a 5 s read timeout, so IPC never blocks the UI thread. |
| Idle lifecycle | A session is dropped only after a 2-minute absence grace; with no session left, the process removes itself after 10 minutes. |

### How it works

```text
Host CLI (Claude Code / OpenCode / Antigravity)
       │
       ▼ (Fire-and-forget hooks)
reporters/*.js
       │
       ▼ (JSON line over Windows named pipe: \\.\pipe\ai-terminal-pet-v1-<8hex>)
AI-Terminal-Pet.exe (Go 1.23, single-instance mutex)
       │
       ├─► internal/pipeserver (32 connections, 5s timeout, OK/ERR response)
       ├─► internal/store (in-memory state, TTL, disk snapshots fallback)
       └─► internal/ui (Win32 layered window, GDI topmost canvas)
```

- **Per-user named pipe**: IPC flows through `\\.\pipe\ai-terminal-pet-v1-<8hex>`, where `<8hex>` is derived from the SHA-256 hash of the user home directory. The exact same pipe-name algorithm is implemented in Go and JavaScript, locked by a cross-language golden test.

- **JSON line protocol**: Sessions transmit one JSON line per message with a 1 MiB payload cap. The server replies with an exact `OK` or `ERR` acknowledgment, and reporters retry until a deadline without treating partial reads as success.

- **On-disk snapshots**: Snapshot files under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\runtime\` provide a fallback channel and serve as the authoritative on-disk record of active sessions.

- **OS observation over heartbeats**: Session existence is decided by operating system observation of the process table and window titles rather than reporter heartbeats. A session remains active as long as its terminal window exists, and removal requires the host to be unobservable for a continuous 2-minute grace period.

- **Disks beat heartbeats**: The disk snapshot is authoritative for session existence: a session that was on disk and is gone is over, while synthetic PIDs from hooks never participate in liveness probing.

- **Connection handling**: The server accommodates 32 concurrent connections with a 5s read timeout, keeping IPC processing off the UI thread.

- **GDI rendering**: A top-down 32bpp DIB section created with CreateDIBSection is painted through a memory DC and handed to the layered window with UpdateLayeredWindow.

### Install

Installation takes about 30 seconds on Windows using PowerShell:

1. Build both executables:
   ```powershell
   go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false -ldflags "-s -w" -o .\bin\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe ./cmd/ai-terminal-pet
   go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false -ldflags "-s -w" -o .\bin\pet-statusline.exe ./cmd/pet-statusline
   ```

2. Run the installer to copy binaries and sync assets:
   ```powershell
   .\scripts\install.ps1
   ```
   The installer lives under `scripts/` rather than at the repository root on purpose: market indexers fetch a root `install.ps1` by name and regex-scan it, and this script legitimately mentions the `HKCU` Run key and a `-Recurse -Force` cleanup. Moving it one level down takes those two false positives off the root without taking any behaviour off the script.

3. Verify that the installation works:
   ```powershell
   & "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\AI-Terminal-Pet\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe" --json
   ```
4. Re-verify the installed artifacts at any time with per-file SHA256 checks:
   ```powershell
   .\scripts\install.ps1 -VerifyOnly
   ```
   It prints `install: verified - 10 file(s) match the repository, 0 warning(s)` and exits 0 only when every deployed artifact matches (the 10 artifacts are the overlay, the statusline shim, `protocol.js`, and the 7 files of the DeepSeek Harness bundle).
   The installer itself stops a running overlay first and waits for the process to release its file handles; a plain file copy over a live binary fails at random, which is what the retry loop and the SHA256 comparison after every copy are for.
5. Optional — put `ai-terminal-pet` on your PATH so you can type the bare command:
   ```powershell
   .\scripts\install.ps1 -AddToPath
   ```
   It writes **only** `HKCU\Environment\Path` (never `HKLM`), backs the previous value up to `<install dir>\path-backup.txt` first, and does nothing if the directory is already listed. **Open a new terminal** for the change to take effect. `-Uninstall` also removes that PATH entry, so uninstalling does not leave a dead entry behind (the previous value is backed up again, this time into `%TEMP%`).
   Without this step the installer does not touch your PATH at all, so keep using the full path `& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\AI-Terminal-Pet\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe" --json`.

Run `ai-terminal-pet --doctor` at any point after installing to self-check the environment, install files, runtime state, pipe, autostart entry, and node availability. To remove the deployed artifacts, run `.\scripts\install.ps1 -Uninstall`; it asks for a typed `yes` confirmation first, refuses unsafe target directories, and accepts `-Force` for unattended removal.

Installing a terminal hook is required for that terminal to report; see the next section to connect your tools.

### Connect your terminal

| Terminal | How to connect | What you get |
|---|---|---|
| OpenCode | Add `file:///C:/path/to/ai-terminal-pet/reporters/opencode.js` to `plugin` in `opencode.json` | Automatic session tracking for tool use, prompt handling, and task completion |
| Claude Code | Add `node <repo>/reporters/claude-hook.js` for `SessionStart`, `SessionEnd`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `Stop`, and `Notification` in `settings.json` | Real-time status updates, tool execution tracking, and permission prompt alerts |
| Antigravity | Set `statusLine.command` to `pet-statusline.exe` and configure `antigravity-hook.js` for agent and tool events | Fast statusline updates, agent state changes, and permission request forwarding |
| DeepSeek Harness | Install the Cordis bundle from `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\bundles\ai-terminal-pet-bridge\` via the plugin manager (`install_bundle`) | turn/start to working, tool/call to tool_use, approval/asked to waiting_permission, tool/result with an error to error, turn/end to idle, process exit to closed |
| Anything else | Run `node reporters/generic.js` with `--source`, `--state`, and `--project` flags | Instant status reporting from any custom script or CLI tool |

Writing your own reporter for a tool that is not listed here needs no source reading: [docs/PROTOCOL.md](docs/PROTOCOL.md) specifies the wire protocol (fields, state semantics, pipe-name derivation, acknowledgment contract, and redaction rules) that a conforming reporter must implement.

The Harness side is a host-only Cordis bundle: it holds no pipe-name, state-set or snapshot logic of its own, it loads the protocol from `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\protocol.js` and delegates everything to it.

The Harness side has a second, self-contained option since `dsh-ai-terminal-pet` `1.1.0`: a standalone DSH plugin package at [`packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet`](packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet), also shipped as a GitHub Release asset. The package is now **1.2.3** (tag `dsh-plugin-v1.2.3`, asset `dsh-ai-terminal-pet-1.2.3.tgz`); 1.2.2, 1.2.1, 1.2.0 and 1.1.0 stay published and immutable but are superseded. 1.2.3 changes the manifests, not the feature set: both manifests now carry a `dsh.marketplace` block that declares the profiles this bundle runs in, which is what a third-party storefront reads before it offers a plugin to its desktop client. 1.2.2 was the previous byte-level change: the installer moved from the repository root into `scripts/`, which edits Go comments, which changes the source digest `vendor/manifest.json` records - so the vendored overlay had to be re-recorded and the package re-packed. Release assets cannot be edited, so a change like that still costs a version - shipping different bytes under an unchanged version is exactly the drift this repository removes. Three install forms are verified end to end (the timings were taken on the 1.1.0 assets; every later release sits at the same URLs with only tag and version changed; a bare `add dsh-ai-terminal-pet` waits on the npm release described below):

```powershell
# from the release tarball: no git clone, no build step
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet/releases/download/dsh-plugin-v1.2.3/dsh-ai-terminal-pet-1.2.3.tgz

# from git, pinned to the release tag
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add "git+https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet.git#dsh-plugin-v1.2.3&path:/packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet"

# from the repository URL: resolves through the root manifest shim
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add github:jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet
```

The repository URL works because the repository root now carries a 59-line `package.json` shim that contains no code: it points `main` at the package, declares `dsh.bundle.patch` as `./packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet/cordis.patch.yml` and limits `files` to that subtree. Without it a host that reads the repository root sees no `dsh.bundle`, installs an empty package and warns `declares no dsh.bundle`. The shim is `private`, so it never occupies the npm name, its `version` tracks the package (`verify.mjs` asserts they are equal, so a bump cannot land in one manifest only), and it carries the same `dsh.catalog` block the package does.

The package ships no lifecycle hooks at all — `prepack` was removed in 1.1.0 — because pnpm runs them for a git dependency and fails an unpinned source with an `allowBuilds` error that never mentions AI Terminal Pet. `vendor/` is committed instead and only verified: `node scripts/vendor.mjs --check` re-hashes the two vendored files and checks `vendor/manifest.json` against them, writing nothing. One form still fails, for a different reason: `git+https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet.git&path:/packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet` without a `#ref` — pnpm concatenates the fragments and asks `ls-remote` for a repository that does not exist, so it reports `repository ... not found`.

1.2.0 also makes the package self-describing: `dsh.catalog` declares a `category` (`tool`), a one-line summary in English and Chinese, and five `capabilities` — `windows-overlay`, `named-pipe`, `session-state`, `tray-icon`, `no-network`. Those capabilities are **self-declared and unenforced**; dsh does not sandbox plugins, so the block describes what the overlay already does rather than granting it permission to do so. `keywords` gained `dsh-plugin`, the tag auto-indexing marketplaces harvest. 1.2.3 adds `dsh.marketplace` next to `dsh.bundle` and `dsh.catalog`: `profiles: ["desktop", "headless", "web"]`, `requiresBuildApproval: false` and `manualSteps: false`. That field is read by third-party registries, not by DSH - the plugin mounts through `dsh.bundle` either way, and this bundle only subscribes to `session/event`, so no profile-specific service is involved: that makes two independent discovery paths — registry review (a reviewed entry merges into `main` and only then appears in the list) and topic/keyword harvesting (no application needed at all). Two marketplaces already harvest automatically: [LivXue/dsh-plugin-shop](https://github.com/LivXue/dsh-plugin-shop) rebuilds daily from npm metadata, and every entry in its published shard is pinned by tarball integrity, so a Git-only package cannot appear there until it reaches npm; [zasenjc/dsh-plugins-store](https://github.com/zasenjc/dsh-plugins-store) syncs every 30 minutes and lists any public repository carrying both the `dsh-plugin` and `deepseek-harness` topics.

Its payload carries a prebuilt overlay and the official `protocol.js`, copied into `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\` on first use **only when they are missing** — an existing install is never overwritten, and the overlay keeps running entirely on its own, so a machine that only wants the pet still needs nothing but `scripts/install.ps1`. Its entry in the [awesome-dsh-plugin](https://github.com/awesome-dsh-plugin/awesome-dsh-plugin) registry ([PR #13937](https://github.com/awesome-dsh-plugin/awesome-dsh-plugin/pull/13937)) passed both upstream checks and was merged on 2026-11-10, so the upstream catalogue lists the entry (the entry file still pinned the 1.2.0 tarball, so a follow-up [PR #14076](https://github.com/awesome-dsh-plugin/awesome-dsh-plugin/pull/14076) points it at the current release, 1.2.3; its predecessor #14063 targeted 1.2.1 and was closed once 1.2.2 packed the corrected bytes, and changing that file always means a pull request against that repository, never an edit here); the rendered catalogue page returned 404 at 16:16Z and became reachable later the same day once the upstream site build finished (`42844452013`, started 15:27:09Z, concluded 16:39:27Z); the catalogue file that DSH's in-app Market actually loads (`plugins.json`, `count` 10119 at the time) contains this repository too, but its `install` command still points at the 1.2.0 release asset until PR #14076 lands. In a comment on the pull request the maintainer explained that he trimmed the merged description himself: for a Harness session the panel only mirrors state and jumps to the DSH window, so approving still happens inside DSH. The [DSH-Plugins-Marketplace](https://github.com/bradeGithub/DSH-Plugins-Marketplace) index picked this repository up automatically; its 18:08:44Z rebuild on 2026-11-10 records `pkg_name`/`version`, the verdict `bundle-plugin`, and now `risk_tier: "safe"` with an empty `risk_flags` list. That is not a favour granted by an allowlist: the scanner only fetches root-level `install.ps1`/`install.sh`/`package.json` and regex-scans them, and the two lines it used to match (`CurrentVersion\Run` and `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force`) moved into `scripts/` together with the installer, so those rules have no input left (the behaviour itself is unchanged). The DSH in-app Discover index accepts an npm version or a git source pinned to a 40-character commit; the npm **credential** problem is resolved (`npm whoami` answers `jjjjjjjjnnjnn` and the name is still free, `npm view` returns E404), but `1.2.3` is **not published yet**, which is why installing by bare package name (`dsh plugin --profile <profile> add dsh-ai-terminal-pet`) does not resolve yet.

Because the plugin index format accepts a git source pinned to a commit, this repository also publishes its own index, so Discover works before npm does. Add this URL once in DSH under Plugins → Discover → index sources:

```text
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet/main/docs/market-index.json
```

[`docs/market-index.json`](docs/market-index.json) is one entry, `dsh-ai-terminal-pet` `1.2.3`, whose install spec is the same `git+...#<commit>&path:/packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet` form that was installed end to end in 2.5 s above, now pinned to the 1.2.3 release commit. It is validated with the host's own `parseMarketIndex` from `@deepseek-ai/dsh-plugin-market-index`: `format: 1`, `en` localized text, declared category and label ids, an https icon pinned to the release commit, and an exact SemVer with a Unix-seconds `publishTimestamp`. When npm publishing is unblocked the same file gains an `npm` source for the next version.

Run `node reporters/generic.js` directly to report from any other CLI or script:

```powershell
node reporters/generic.js --source=aider --state=working --project="$PWD"
node reporters/generic.js --source=codex --state=waiting_permission --reason=approve
echo '{"state":"error","reason":"build failed"}' | node reporters/generic.js --source=ci --stdin
```

- `--source`: sets the reporter identity name.
- `--state`: sets one of the seven official session states.
- `--stdin`: parses a JSON payload piped directly from standard input.

### Control it from a script

The commands below assume `ai-terminal-pet` is on your PATH (install step 5, `.\scripts\install.ps1 -AddToPath`). If you skipped that step, prefix every command with the full path instead: `& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\AI-Terminal-Pet\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe" --json`.

| Command | Effect |
|---|---|
| `ai-terminal-pet` | Start the overlay (no-op if already running) |
| `ai-terminal-pet --show` | Reveal the running overlay |
| `ai-terminal-pet --toggle` | Switch between compact and expanded views |
| `ai-terminal-pet --reset` | Re-anchor to the screen edge at 100% zoom |
| `ai-terminal-pet --settings` | Open the settings window |
| `ai-terminal-pet --quit` | Stop the running overlay |
| `ai-terminal-pet --json` | Print the current sessions as JSON (add `--pretty` for formatted output) |
| `ai-terminal-pet --doctor` | Run 9 environment and install checks; exit code 1 when a check fails. Again: needs the install directory on PATH, or call it by full path |
| `ai-terminal-pet --autostart` | Report the run-at-logon state |
| `ai-terminal-pet --autostart=on` | Enable run at logon |
| `ai-terminal-pet --autostart=off` | Disable run at logon |
| `ai-terminal-pet --version` | Print version information |
| `ai-terminal-pet --help` | Print CLI usage help |

Run `--json` to inspect active sessions directly from scripts or shell status lines:

```powershell
ai-terminal-pet --json --pretty
```

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": "ai-terminal-pet.v1",
  "state": "waiting_permission",
  "count": 2,
  "generatedAt": "2026-11-09T21:30:00Z",
  "sessions": [{"project": "ai-terminal-pet", "state": "waiting_permission", "source": "claude-hook"}]}
```

The `--json` command never blocks on a GUI process because it reads session snapshots directly from disk.

### Safety

Terminal hooks run inside your development environment, so their boundaries are strict:

- **Fail-fast reporters**: Reporters run fire-and-forget, catch errors internally, and never throw exceptions or block your host CLI. Any reporter failure terminates silently without interrupting user keystrokes or host terminal operations.

- **Auto-approve disabled by default**: The auto-approve feature starts turned off; activating it requires explicit configuration. A terminal hook that cannot read the configuration file automatically defaults to off.

- **Configurable veto window**: When auto-approve is active, permission prompts display a draining bar on the expanded panel; a single tap denies the prompt, while silence approves after the countdown. Ordinary tool calls without permission prompts are never delayed.

- **Dangerous-command denylist**: Destructive commands never auto-approve and always fall back to manual prompts, blocking patterns such as `rm -rf`, `git push --force`, `format C:`, `rd /s`, and `shutdown /s`. A matched command forces manual review in the terminal.

- **Zero network activity**: The application makes no network calls, contains no telemetry, and stores all configuration and runtime snapshots under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\`. No code or logs leave your local machine.

- **Per-user ACL protection**: The named pipe DACL `"D:P(A;;GRGW;;;OW)(A;;GRGW;;;SY)"` grants read/write access to the owner of the pipe and to LocalSystem only, and nothing for any other account on the machine. Other local users therefore cannot connect and cannot occupy the pipe name.

### Known limits

- **Windows only**: The overlay relies directly on Win32 layered windows and Windows named pipes; macOS and Linux are not supported.

- **Process creation overhead**: Antivirus scanning hooks can make each Node.js process launch take roughly 1s; using the native `pet-statusline.exe` shim or adding an AV exclusion for the install folder reduces this latency. The delay comes from process scanning rather than application code.

- **Named-pipe squatting**: Same-user pipe preemption is mitigated by acquiring a named mutex first, but it is not completely eliminated. A full challenge-response handshake remains documented for future hardening.

- **Auto-approve countdown restart**: Changing the auto-approve countdown duration requires an overlay restart, while all other settings hot-reload automatically.

- **No pixel regression tests**: Pure UI logic, hit testing, and layout bounding boxes are unit-tested, but automated visual pixel regression testing is not in place. Visual verification relies on the PNG preview generator.

- **Window focus granularity**: Session jump focusing resolves tabs in Windows Terminal, but classic conhost windows and VS Code integrated terminals resolve only to the parent window level.

### Roadmap

- **Native hook binary**: A unified `pet-hook.exe` executable to eliminate per-event Node.js spawns for Claude Code and Antigravity (planned).

- **Cross-platform support**: Extracting the UI layer behind a presenter interface with Unix domain socket transport for macOS and Linux (not started).

- **Binary size reduction**: Bring the main executable under 2.5 MiB (currently 4.17 MiB) by stripping reflection metadata and dropping unused packages, and replace the regexp-based redaction in pet-statusline with a hand-written scanner.

Shipped after v0.9.0: the wire protocol specification ([docs/PROTOCOL.md](docs/PROTOCOL.md)) and the `ai-terminal-pet --doctor` self-check command, so both items previously listed here as pending are now available.

Shipped after v0.9.0 as a distribution channel, not just a repository: the Harness bridge is now also a standalone DSH plugin package (`dsh-ai-terminal-pet` 1.2.3, GitHub Release tag `dsh-plugin-v1.2.3`, replacing the superseded 1.2.2, 1.2.1, 1.2.0 and 1.1.0). It also declares `dsh.marketplace.profiles` so a desktop-facing storefront offers it to the desktop profile instead of hiding it. It installs from the release tarball, from git pinned to that tag, or straight from the repository URL through the root manifest shim, and it describes itself to storefronts through `dsh.catalog`. Its registry entry ([PR #13937](https://github.com/awesome-dsh-plugin/awesome-dsh-plugin/pull/13937)) was merged on 2026-11-10, and the upstream README already lists the entry under "Notifications & Integrations"; the maintainer trimmed one sentence while merging, because for a Harness session the panel only mirrors state and jumps to the Harness window - approvals still happen inside DSH. Merged into `main` is not the same as visible in a market - but visibility did arrive: the catalogue page returned 404 at 16:16Z and 200 after the upstream site build finished at 16:39:27Z, and `plugins.json` (`count` 10119 to 10230) now lists this repository, tho

decision.reason: The repository is already represented by catalog id jjjjjjjjnnjnn-ai-terminal-pet; this additional manifest or newer fixed-source snapshot is not a separate repository-level catalog entry. Existing retained catalog snapshots are not re-certified or replaced by this duplicate decision.

# ai-terminal-pet

Stop glancing across terminal windows to track agent states. It costs one small executable with no account and no cloud.

![ai-terminal-pet](docs/assets/hero.png)

![Platform](https://img.shields.io/badge/platform-Windows-blue) ![Go](https://img.shields.io/badge/go-1.23-00ADD8) ![Version](https://img.shields.io/badge/version-0.9.0-blue)
![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-green) ![Size](https://img.shields.io/badge/size-4.17%20MiB-blue) ![Dependencies](https://img.shields.io/badge/dependencies-3-informational) ![Tests](https://img.shields.io/badge/tests-154-brightgreen)

> 🇬🇧 [English](#english)  ·  🇨🇳 [中文](#中文)

---

## English

### The problem

You run Claude Code, OpenCode, or Antigravity in multiple terminal windows at once. A background task prompts for permission to execute a tool, but you are focused in another window and never notice the prompt.

Fourteen minutes later, you switch back only to discover that your build has been sitting idle the entire time. Glancing across multiple terminal tabs wastes focus and breaks your concentration.

ai-terminal-pet anchors a 56px strip to the screen edge. It aggregates your sessions in real time, pulses when an agent needs permission, and displays which project is waiting and for how long.

The table below contrasts the everyday workflow before and after using the overlay:

| Context | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Multiple terminals | Four terminal windows open; you lose track of which window needs attention. | One 56px strip on the edge of the screen aggregates every active session. |
| Blocked build | You find out a build was blocked on a permission prompt fourteen minutes ago. | The overlay pulses immediately and shows which project is waiting and for how long. |
| Context switching | You click across tabs to check whether builds and tasks are still running. | A single glance reveals current states without touching your keyboard or mouse. |

### What it looks like

![Compact strip](docs/assets/overlay-compact.png)
*Compact strip: pulsing state orb with status glyph, session count, state word, and waiting project name.*

![Expanded list](docs/assets/overlay-expanded.png)
*Expanded list: active sessions showing per-row project name, state, source hook, and relative time.*

![Many sessions](docs/assets/overlay-expanded-many.png)
*Expanded list with many sessions: six session rows followed by the overflow line showing remaining sessions.*

![Auto-approve countdown](docs/assets/overlay-auto-approve.png)
*Auto-approve countdown: draining bar with "Allow (5s)" prompt allowing manual veto before automatic permission approval.*

---

### Features

The table below outlines the core capabilities and exact runtime parameters of the application:

| Feature | What it actually does |
|---|---|
| State aggregation | Aggregates sessions across 7 states (`idle`, `thinking`, `working`, `tool_use`, `waiting_permission`, `error`, `closed`), showing the highest-priority state across all active sessions. |
| Compact and expanded panels | Compact panel occupies 56x156 logical pixels anchored to a screen edge; clicking expands to 200 px wide, displaying 1–6 rows before adding an overflow line. |
| Whole-panel gestures | Click anywhere toggles compact and expanded views, drag anywhere moves 1:1 with the cursor, and mouse wheel adjusts zoom between 65% and 160%. |
| Edge retract | Slides mostly off-screen when docked at an edge leaving a thin sliver; hovering restores it, while waiting_permission or error states override retraction to remain visible. |
| Tray menu | Right-click tray menu toggles visibility, resets position and zoom, opens settings, switches language, toggles autostart, and configures auto-approve. |
| Settings window | Native three-tab window (General, Sound, Sessions) where every change persists immediately to `config.json` without an OK button. |
| Synthesized alert tones | Generates 44.1 kHz 16-bit mono PCM WAV tones in memory across four sound schemes (`chime`, `bell`, `soft`, `pulse`), with separate gates for waiting, error, and finish. |
| Per-session alerts | Fires Windows tray notification balloons and audio alerts on transitions into `waiting_permission`, `error`, or finish states. |
| Auto-approve and denylist | Provides a 5-second veto window on permission prompts where a tap denies and silence approves; blocks commands matching the dangerous-command denylist. |
| Jump to terminal | Walks session process ancestry and matches window titles to bring the waiting terminal window or tab to the foreground. |
| Scriptable CLI | Outputs structured session state via `ai-terminal-pet --json` by reading disk snapshots, avoiding blocking on GUI processes. |
| Single instance | A named mutex makes a second launch activate the running overlay instead of starting another one. |
| Connection capacity | The pipe server accepts 32 concurrent connections with a 5 s read timeout, so IPC never blocks the UI thread. |
| Idle lifecycle | A session is dropped only after a 2-minute absence grace; with no session left, the process removes itself after 10 minutes. |

### How it works

```text
Host CLI (Claude Code / OpenCode / Antigravity)
       │
       ▼ (Fire-and-forget hooks)
reporters/*.js
       │
       ▼ (JSON line over Windows named pipe: \\.\pipe\ai-terminal-pet-v1-<8hex>)
AI-Terminal-Pet.exe (Go 1.23, single-instance mutex)
       │
       ├─► internal/pipeserver (32 connections, 5s timeout, OK/ERR response)
       ├─► internal/store (in-memory state, TTL, disk snapshots fallback)
       └─► internal/ui (Win32 layered window, GDI topmost canvas)
```

- **Per-user named pipe**: IPC flows through `\\.\pipe\ai-terminal-pet-v1-<8hex>`, where `<8hex>` is derived from the SHA-256 hash of the user home directory. The exact same pipe-name algorithm is implemented in Go and JavaScript, locked by a cross-language golden test.

- **JSON line protocol**: Sessions transmit one JSON line per message with a 1 MiB payload cap. The server replies with an exact `OK` or `ERR` acknowledgment, and reporters retry until a deadline without treating partial reads as success.

- **On-disk snapshots**: Snapshot files under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\runtime\` provide a fallback channel and serve as the authoritative on-disk record of active sessions.

- **OS observation over heartbeats**: Session existence is decided by operating system observation of the process table and window titles rather than reporter heartbeats. A session remains active as long as its terminal window exists, and removal requires the host to be unobservable for a continuous 2-minute grace period.

- **Disks beat heartbeats**: The disk snapshot is authoritative for session existence: a session that was on disk and is gone is over, while synthetic PIDs from hooks never participate in liveness probing.

- **Connection handling**: The server accommodates 32 concurrent connections with a 5s read timeout, keeping IPC processing off the UI thread.

- **GDI rendering**: A top-down 32bpp DIB section created with CreateDIBSection is painted through a memory DC and handed to the layered window with UpdateLayeredWindow.

### Install

Installation takes about 30 seconds on Windows using PowerShell:

1. Build both executables:
   ```powershell
   go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false -ldflags "-s -w" -o .\bin\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe ./cmd/ai-terminal-pet
   go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false -ldflags "-s -w" -o .\bin\pet-statusline.exe ./cmd/pet-statusline
   ```

2. Run the installer to copy binaries and sync assets:
   ```powershell
   .\scripts\install.ps1
   ```
   The installer lives under `scripts/` rather than at the repository root on purpose: market indexers fetch a root `install.ps1` by name and regex-scan it, and this script legitimately mentions the `HKCU` Run key and a `-Recurse -Force` cleanup. Moving it one level down takes those two false positives off the root without taking any behaviour off the script.

3. Verify that the installation works:
   ```powershell
   & "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\AI-Terminal-Pet\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe" --json
   ```
4. Re-verify the installed artifacts at any time with per-file SHA256 checks:
   ```powershell
   .\scripts\install.ps1 -VerifyOnly
   ```
   It prints `install: verified - 10 file(s) match the repository, 0 warning(s)` and exits 0 only when every deployed artifact matches (the 10 artifacts are the overlay, the statusline shim, `protocol.js`, and the 7 files of the DeepSeek Harness bundle).
   The installer itself stops a running overlay first and waits for the process to release its file handles; a plain file copy over a live binary fails at random, which is what the retry loop and the SHA256 comparison after every copy are for.
5. Optional — put `ai-terminal-pet` on your PATH so you can type the bare command:
   ```powershell
   .\scripts\install.ps1 -AddToPath
   ```
   It writes **only** `HKCU\Environment\Path` (never `HKLM`), backs the previous value up to `<install dir>\path-backup.txt` first, and does nothing if the directory is already listed. **Open a new terminal** for the change to take effect. `-Uninstall` also removes that PATH entry, so uninstalling does not leave a dead entry behind (the previous value is backed up again, this time into `%TEMP%`).
   Without this step the installer does not touch your PATH at all, so keep using the full path `& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\AI-Terminal-Pet\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe" --json`.

Run `ai-terminal-pet --doctor` at any point after installing to self-check the environment, install files, runtime state, pipe, autostart entry, and node availability. To remove the deployed artifacts, run `.\scripts\install.ps1 -Uninstall`; it asks for a typed `yes` confirmation first, refuses unsafe target directories, and accepts `-Force` for unattended removal.

Installing a terminal hook is required for that terminal to report; see the next section to connect your tools.

### Connect your terminal

| Terminal | How to connect | What you get |
|---|---|---|
| OpenCode | Add `file:///C:/path/to/ai-terminal-pet/reporters/opencode.js` to `plugin` in `opencode.json` | Automatic session tracking for tool use, prompt handling, and task completion |
| Claude Code | Add `node <repo>/reporters/claude-hook.js` for `SessionStart`, `SessionEnd`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `Stop`, and `Notification` in `settings.json` | Real-time status updates, tool execution tracking, and permission prompt alerts |
| Antigravity | Set `statusLine.command` to `pet-statusline.exe` and configure `antigravity-hook.js` for agent and tool events | Fast statusline updates, agent state changes, and permission request forwarding |
| DeepSeek Harness | Install the Cordis bundle from `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\bundles\ai-terminal-pet-bridge\` via the plugin manager (`install_bundle`) | turn/start to working, tool/call to tool_use, approval/asked to waiting_permission, tool/result with an error to error, turn/end to idle, process exit to closed |
| Anything else | Run `node reporters/generic.js` with `--source`, `--state`, and `--project` flags | Instant status reporting from any custom script or CLI tool |

Writing your own reporter for a tool that is not listed here needs no source reading: [docs/PROTOCOL.md](docs/PROTOCOL.md) specifies the wire protocol (fields, state semantics, pipe-name derivation, acknowledgment contract, and redaction rules) that a conforming reporter must implement.

The Harness side is a host-only Cordis bundle: it holds no pipe-name, state-set or snapshot logic of its own, it loads the protocol from `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\protocol.js` and delegates everything to it.

The Harness side has a second, self-contained option since `dsh-ai-terminal-pet` `1.1.0`: a standalone DSH plugin package at [`packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet`](packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet), also shipped as a GitHub Release asset. The package is now **1.2.3** (tag `dsh-plugin-v1.2.3`, asset `dsh-ai-terminal-pet-1.2.3.tgz`); 1.2.2, 1.2.1, 1.2.0 and 1.1.0 stay published and immutable but are superseded. 1.2.3 changes the manifests, not the feature set: both manifests now carry a `dsh.marketplace` block that declares the profiles this bundle runs in, which is what a third-party storefront reads before it offers a plugin to its desktop client. 1.2.2 was the previous byte-level change: the installer moved from the repository root into `scripts/`, which edits Go comments, which changes the source digest `vendor/manifest.json` records - so the vendored overlay had to be re-recorded and the package re-packed. Release assets cannot be edited, so a change like that still costs a version - shipping different bytes under an unchanged version is exactly the drift this repository removes. Three install forms are verified end to end (the timings were taken on the 1.1.0 assets; every later release sits at the same URLs with only tag and version changed; a bare `add dsh-ai-terminal-pet` waits on the npm release described below):

```powershell
# from the release tarball: no git clone, no build step
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet/releases/download/dsh-plugin-v1.2.3/dsh-ai-terminal-pet-1.2.3.tgz

# from git, pinned to the release tag
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add "git+https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet.git#dsh-plugin-v1.2.3&path:/packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet"

# from the repository URL: resolves through the root manifest shim
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add github:jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet
```

The repository URL works because the repository root now carries a 59-line `package.json` shim that contains no code: it points `main` at the package, declares `dsh.bundle.patch` as `./packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet/cordis.patch.yml` and limits `files` to that subtree. Without it a host that reads the repository root sees no `dsh.bundle`, installs an empty package and warns `declares no dsh.bundle`. The shim is `private`, so it never occupies the npm name, its `version` tracks the package (`verify.mjs` asserts they are equal, so a bump cannot land in one manifest only), and it carries the same `dsh.catalog` block the package does.

The package ships no lifecycle hooks at all — `prepack` was removed in 1.1.0 — because pnpm runs them for a git dependency and fails an unpinned source with an `allowBuilds` error that never mentions AI Terminal Pet. `vendor/` is committed instead and only verified: `node scripts/vendor.mjs --check` re-hashes the two vendored files and checks `vendor/manifest.json` against them, writing nothing. One form still fails, for a different reason: `git+https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet.git&path:/packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet` without a `#ref` — pnpm concatenates the fragments and asks `ls-remote` for a repository that does not exist, so it reports `repository ... not found`.

1.2.0 also makes the package self-describing: `dsh.catalog` declares a `category` (`tool`), a one-line summary in English and Chinese, and five `capabilities` — `windows-overlay`, `named-pipe`, `session-state`, `tray-icon`, `no-network`. Those capabilities are **self-declared and unenforced**; dsh does not sandbox plugins, so the block describes what the overlay already does rather than granting it permission to do so. `keywords` gained `dsh-plugin`, the tag auto-indexing marketplaces harvest. 1.2.3 adds `dsh.marketplace` next to `dsh.bundle` and `dsh.catalog`: `profiles: ["desktop", "headless", "web"]`, `requiresBuildApproval: false` and `manualSteps: false`. That field is read by third-party registries, not by DSH - the plugin mounts through `dsh.bundle` either way, and this bundle only subscribes to `session/event`, so no profile-specific service is involved: that makes two independent discovery paths — registry review (a reviewed entry merges into `main` and only then appears in the list) and topic/keyword harvesting (no application needed at all). Two marketplaces already harvest automatically: [LivXue/dsh-plugin-shop](https://github.com/LivXue/dsh-plugin-shop) rebuilds daily from npm metadata, and every entry in its published shard is pinned by tarball integrity, so a Git-only package cannot appear there until it reaches npm; [zasenjc/dsh-plugins-store](https://github.com/zasenjc/dsh-plugins-store) syncs every 30 minutes and lists any public repository carrying both the `dsh-plugin` and `deepseek-harness` topics.

Its payload carries a prebuilt overlay and the official `protocol.js`, copied into `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\` on first use **only when they are missing** — an existing install is never overwritten, and the overlay keeps running entirely on its own, so a machine that only wants the pet still needs nothing but `scripts/install.ps1`. Its entry in the [awesome-dsh-plugin](https://github.com/awesome-dsh-plugin/awesome-dsh-plugin) registry ([PR #13937](https://github.com/awesome-dsh-plugin/awesome-dsh-plugin/pull/13937)) passed both upstream checks and was merged on 2026-11-10, so the upstream catalogue lists the entry (the entry file still pinned the 1.2.0 tarball, so a follow-up [PR #14076](https://github.com/awesome-dsh-plugin/awesome-dsh-plugin/pull/14076) points it at the current release, 1.2.3; its predecessor #14063 targeted 1.2.1 and was closed once 1.2.2 packed the corrected bytes, and changing that file always means a pull request against that repository, never an edit here); the rendered catalogue page returned 404 at 16:16Z and became reachable later the same day once the upstream site build finished (`42844452013`, started 15:27:09Z, concluded 16:39:27Z); the catalogue file that DSH's in-app Market actually loads (`plugins.json`, `count` 10119 at the time) contains this repository too, but its `install` command still points at the 1.2.0 release asset until PR #14076 lands. In a comment on the pull request the maintainer explained that he trimmed the merged description himself: for a Harness session the panel only mirrors state and jumps to the DSH window, so approving still happens inside DSH. The [DSH-Plugins-Marketplace](https://github.com/bradeGithub/DSH-Plugins-Marketplace) index picked this repository up automatically; its 18:08:44Z rebuild on 2026-11-10 records `pkg_name`/`version`, the verdict `bundle-plugin`, and now `risk_tier: "safe"` with an empty `risk_flags` list. That is not a favour granted by an allowlist: the scanner only fetches root-level `install.ps1`/`install.sh`/`package.json` and regex-scans them, and the two lines it used to match (`CurrentVersion\Run` and `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force`) moved into `scripts/` together with the installer, so those rules have no input left (the behaviour itself is unchanged). The DSH in-app Discover index accepts an npm version or a git source pinned to a 40-character commit; the npm **credential** problem is resolved (`npm whoami` answers `jjjjjjjjnnjnn` and the name is still free, `npm view` returns E404), but `1.2.3` is **not published yet**, which is why installing by bare package name (`dsh plugin --profile <profile> add dsh-ai-terminal-pet`) does not resolve yet.

Because the plugin index format accepts a git source pinned to a commit, this repository also publishes its own index, so Discover works before npm does. Add this URL once in DSH under Plugins → Discover → index sources:

```text
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet/main/docs/market-index.json
```

[`docs/market-index.json`](docs/market-index.json) is one entry, `dsh-ai-terminal-pet` `1.2.3`, whose install spec is the same `git+...#<commit>&path:/packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet` form that was installed end to end in 2.5 s above, now pinned to the 1.2.3 release commit. It is validated with the host's own `parseMarketIndex` from `@deepseek-ai/dsh-plugin-market-index`: `format: 1`, `en` localized text, declared category and label ids, an https icon pinned to the release commit, and an exact SemVer with a Unix-seconds `publishTimestamp`. When npm publishing is unblocked the same file gains an `npm` source for the next version.

Run `node reporters/generic.js` directly to report from any other CLI or script:

```powershell
node reporters/generic.js --source=aider --state=working --project="$PWD"
node reporters/generic.js --source=codex --state=waiting_permission --reason=approve
echo '{"state":"error","reason":"build failed"}' | node reporters/generic.js --source=ci --stdin
```

- `--source`: sets the reporter identity name.
- `--state`: sets one of the seven official session states.
- `--stdin`: parses a JSON payload piped directly from standard input.

### Control it from a script

The commands below assume `ai-terminal-pet` is on your PATH (install step 5, `.\scripts\install.ps1 -AddToPath`). If you skipped that step, prefix every command with the full path instead: `& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\AI-Terminal-Pet\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe" --json`.

| Command | Effect |
|---|---|
| `ai-terminal-pet` | Start the overlay (no-op if already running) |
| `ai-terminal-pet --show` | Reveal the running overlay |
| `ai-terminal-pet --toggle` | Switch between compact and expanded views |
| `ai-terminal-pet --reset` | Re-anchor to the screen edge at 100% zoom |
| `ai-terminal-pet --settings` | Open the settings window |
| `ai-terminal-pet --quit` | Stop the running overlay |
| `ai-terminal-pet --json` | Print the current sessions as JSON (add `--pretty` for formatted output) |
| `ai-terminal-pet --doctor` | Run 9 environment and install checks; exit code 1 when a check fails. Again: needs the install directory on PATH, or call it by full path |
| `ai-terminal-pet --autostart` | Report the run-at-logon state |
| `ai-terminal-pet --autostart=on` | Enable run at logon |
| `ai-terminal-pet --autostart=off` | Disable run at logon |
| `ai-terminal-pet --version` | Print version information |
| `ai-terminal-pet --help` | Print CLI usage help |

Run `--json` to inspect active sessions directly from scripts or shell status lines:

```powershell
ai-terminal-pet --json --pretty
```

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": "ai-terminal-pet.v1",
  "state": "waiting_permission",
  "count": 2,
  "generatedAt": "2026-11-09T21:30:00Z",
  "sessions": [{"project": "ai-terminal-pet", "state": "waiting_permission", "source": "claude-hook"}]}
```

The `--json` command never blocks on a GUI process because it reads session snapshots directly from disk.

### Safety

Terminal hooks run inside your development environment, so their boundaries are strict:

- **Fail-fast reporters**: Reporters run fire-and-forget, catch errors internally, and never throw exceptions or block your host CLI. Any reporter failure terminates silently without interrupting user keystrokes or host terminal operations.

- **Auto-approve disabled by default**: The auto-approve feature starts turned off; activating it requires explicit configuration. A terminal hook that cannot read the configuration file automatically defaults to off.

- **Configurable veto window**: When auto-approve is active, permission prompts display a draining bar on the expanded panel; a single tap denies the prompt, while silence approves after the countdown. Ordinary tool calls without permission prompts are never delayed.

- **Dangerous-command denylist**: Destructive commands never auto-approve and always fall back to manual prompts, blocking patterns such as `rm -rf`, `git push --force`, `format C:`, `rd /s`, and `shutdown /s`. A matched command forces manual review in the terminal.

- **Zero network activity**: The application makes no network calls, contains no telemetry, and stores all configuration and runtime snapshots under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\`. No code or logs leave your local machine.

- **Per-user ACL protection**: The named pipe DACL `"D:P(A;;GRGW;;;OW)(A;;GRGW;;;SY)"` grants read/write access to the owner of the pipe and to LocalSystem only, and nothing for any other account on the machine. Other local users therefore cannot connect and cannot occupy the pipe name.

### Known limits

- **Windows only**: The overlay relies directly on Win32 layered windows and Windows named pipes; macOS and Linux are not supported.

- **Process creation overhead**: Antivirus scanning hooks can make each Node.js process launch take roughly 1s; using the native `pet-statusline.exe` shim or adding an AV exclusion for the install folder reduces this latency. The delay comes from process scanning rather than application code.

- **Named-pipe squatting**: Same-user pipe preemption is mitigated by acquiring a named mutex first, but it is not completely eliminated. A full challenge-response handshake remains documented for future hardening.

- **Auto-approve countdown restart**: Changing the auto-approve countdown duration requires an overlay restart, while all other settings hot-reload automatically.

- **No pixel regression tests**: Pure UI logic, hit testing, and layout bounding boxes are unit-tested, but automated visual pixel regression testing is not in place. Visual verification relies on the PNG preview generator.

- **Window focus granularity**: Session jump focusing resolves tabs in Windows Terminal, but classic conhost windows and VS Code integrated terminals resolve only to the parent window level.

### Roadmap

- **Native hook binary**: A unified `pet-hook.exe` executable to eliminate per-event Node.js spawns for Claude Code and Antigravity (planned).

- **Cross-platform support**: Extracting the UI layer behind a presenter interface with Unix domain socket transport for macOS and Linux (not started).

- **Binary size reduction**: Bring the main executable under 2.5 MiB (currently 4.17 MiB) by stripping reflection metadata and dropping unused packages, and replace the regexp-based redaction in pet-statusline with a hand-written scanner.

Shipped after v0.9.0: the wire protocol specification ([docs/PROTOCOL.md](docs/PROTOCOL.md)) and the `ai-terminal-pet --doctor` self-check command, so both items previously listed here as pending are now available.

Shipped after v0.9.0 as a distribution channel, not just a repository: the Harness bridge is now also a standalone DSH plugin package (`dsh-ai-terminal-pet` 1.2.3, GitHub Release tag `dsh-plugin-v1.2.3`, replacing the superseded 1.2.2, 1.2.1, 1.2.0 and 1.1.0). It also declares `dsh.marketplace.profiles` so a desktop-facing storefront offers it to the desktop profile instead of hiding it. It installs from the release tarball, from git pinned to that tag, or straight from the repository URL through the root manifest shim, and it describes itself to storefronts through `dsh.catalog`. Its registry entry ([PR #13937](https://github.com/awesome-dsh-plugin/awesome-dsh-plugin/pull/13937)) was merged on 2026-11-10, and the upstream README already lists the entry under "Notifications & Integrations"; the maintainer trimmed one sentence while merging, because for a Harness session the panel only mirrors state and jumps to the Harness window - approvals still happen inside DSH. Merged into `main` is not the same as visible in a market - but visibility did arrive: the catalogue page returned 404 at 16:16Z and 200 after the upstream site build finished at 16:39:27Z, and `plugins.json` (`count` 10119 to 10230) now lists this repository, though the `install` command in it still points at the 1.2.0 asset until the follow-up PR #14076 lands. The topic/keyword path needs no application at all, and the DSH-Plugins-Marketplace rebuild of 2026-11-10 has already moved the entry to `bundle-plugin` with no risk tier attached - not the same as rated safe, because that scanner only ever fetched the repository-root `install.ps1` and never re-scanned the tree after the installer moved into `scripts/`. The DSH in-app Discover index needs an npm release or a commit-pinned git source; npm's credential problem is resolved and publishing 1.2.3 is the next step.

### Non-goals

- No accounts, no cloud sync, no telemetry; everything stays in `%LOCALAPPDATA%`.
- Not a terminal multiplexer and not a replacement for your terminal — it only tells you which session wants attention.

### License

Distributed under the MIT License. See [LICENSE](LICENSE) for details. Third-party dependencies are used as libraries only with zero vendored code: github.com/Microsoft/go-winio (MIT), github.com/lxn/win (BSD-style), and golang.org/x/sys (BSD-style).

### Develop from source

Run verification commands when modifying code:

```powershell
go vet ./...
go test -count=1 ./...
# node --check only validates the FIRST file it is given, so check each one:
for f in reporters/*.js; do node --check "$f"; done
node integrations/deepseek-harness/verify.mjs
$env:PET_PREVIEW_DIR = "$env:TEMP\petpreview"
```

`-buildvcs=false` in the two build commands is not decoration: it strips the VCS stamp, which encodes the commit and working-tree state at build time. Two builds of the same source therefore produce identical bytes, on any machine and at any date. Without it a rebuild of `pet-statusline.exe` weighs 3,644,416 B instead of 3,643,392 B, so `.\scripts\install.ps1 -VerifyOnly` — which compares the installed files against the copy in your working tree — reports a false failure whenever one side carries the stamp and the other does not. The binaries themselves are not committed (`bin/` is ignored); you always build them locally.

`.\scripts\install.ps1 -VerifyOnly` re-checks every installed artifact against the recorded SHA256 list, and `.\scripts\install.ps1 -Uninstall` removes them. CI runs the same gates on every push: `.github/workflows/ci.yml` builds on `windows-latest` and fails the job on any `gofmt -l` output, `go vet` finding, failing `go test -count=1 ./...`, unsuccessful `go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false -ldflags "-s -w"` build, any reporter failing its own `node --check`, or failed `node integrations/deepseek-harness/verify.mjs`, `node packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet/scripts/vendor.mjs --

# dsh-ai-terminal-pet

A DeepSeek Harness (DSH) Cordis bundle that mirrors Harness session state onto
the [AI Terminal Pet](https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet) desktop
overlay: a small always-on-top Win32 pet that shows which sessions are working,
which one is waiting for your approval, which failed, and which finished.

The package ships the overlay binary and the official reporter protocol module
inside the tarball, so a single market install is enough to get a pet on screen.
No npm dependencies, no install scripts, no network calls at runtime (unless the
maintainer pins a release in lib/release-pins.json, see below).

## What it does

| Harness event | Overlay state |
| --- | --- |
| turn/start, agent/inbox/claimed, agent/status running | working |
| tool/call | tool_use |
| approval/asked, approval/request | waiting_permission |
| tool/result with error, command/done error, agent/error | error |
| turn/end, command/done success | idle |
| Harness process exit | closed |

The overlay then plays an alert tone, shows a tray balloon on those transitions
and its one-click jump button targets the Harness window. Plugin reload (HMR)
disposes the listeners but deliberately does not close sessions: only a real
process exit means the conversation is over.

The bundle's entry in the [awesome-dsh-plugin](https://github.com/awesome-dsh-plugin/awesome-dsh-plugin)
registry ([PR #13937](https://github.com/awesome-dsh-plugin/awesome-dsh-plugin/pull/13937)) was
merged on 2026-11-10, and that repository's README lists it. Being merged is not the same as
being visible in a market, and initially it was not: the entry page answered 404 and the catalog
file behind DSH's own Plugins -> Market did not contain this repository while the upstream site
build was still queued. That build finished (run 42844452013, 16:39:27Z), the entry page now
answers 200, and the catalog (`count` 10119 -> 10230) lists this repository - so it can be found
in that market. The entry's `install` command, however, is generated from the pinned `tarball`
and pointed at the 1.2.0 asset; a follow-up PR moves it to the current release, which is 1.2.3.
Changing that file always means a pull request against that repository, never an edit here.

The other route needs no application at all: third-party markets harvest GitHub
repositories carrying the `dsh-plugin` topic (this repository has it) together with
a root `package.json` that declares `name` and `dsh.bundle`. That is exactly why
the repository root carries a shim manifest — `dsh plugin add github:owner/repo`
reads the root manifest, and without one the install resolves to a 0.0.0
dependency that mounts nothing.

The package describes itself to those storefronts through `dsh.catalog`: a
category, a one-line summary in both languages, and the capabilities it uses.
Capabilities are self-declared and never checked — DSH does not sandbox plugins —
so read them as a description, not a permission grant.
The bundle is Windows only and declares `dsh.bundle.platforms: ["win32"]`, so
other platforms show it as unsupported instead of installing it.

It also declares `dsh.marketplace` (`profiles: ["desktop", "headless", "web"]`,
`requiresBuildApproval: false`, `manualSteps: false`). DSH itself never reads
that field - the bundle mounts through `dsh.bundle` either way - but storefronts
that sort entries by profile do: without it a registry falls back to a
headless-or-web guess and a desktop client hides the entry.

Manually, from a terminal, into a profile you own — use the release tarball or
pin the release tag. Both are verified end to end:

```sh
# release tarball: no clone, no Go toolchain
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet/releases/download/dsh-plugin-v1.2.3/dsh-ai-terminal-pet-1.2.3.tgz

# git source, pinned to the release tag
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add "git+https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet.git#dsh-plugin-v1.2.3&path:/packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet"
```

Do not hand pnpm a bare repository URL. pnpm resolves a git dependency by
running the package's lifecycle scripts, and it blocks those for unpinned
git sources until you copy the `allowBuilds` key it prints into your profile's
`pnpm-workspace.yaml`; the failure message never mentions AI Terminal Pet. The
package therefore ships no lifecycle hook, and its vendored overlay is a
committed file rather than a build product. `vendor/manifest.json` records the
SHA-256 of that file, the SHA-256 of the Go sources it was built from, and the
Go version that produced it, so a stale or hand-edited vendor directory fails a
check instead of shipping quietly.

The GitHub paths above need no npm. Installing by package name
(`add dsh-ai-terminal-pet`) starts working once the package is published to the
npm registry; until then use one of the two commands above.

`add` is the whole install: the profile records the dependency, and the bundle
declares itself through `dsh.bundle.patch`, so no separate `enable` step exists.
The profile you add it to has to be the one Harness boots.

Two profiles are special. The reserved `desktop` profile is rejected by the
standalone `dsh` CLI (`profile "desktop" is managed exclusively by the Electron
application`); the Desktop app's own bundled CLI does accept it, and the in-app
plugin manager is the supported path there. Any other profile name is yours.

If the app reports restart-required after enabling the bundle, restart Harness.

## What it writes on disk

First use in a Harness process copies two files, and only when they are missing:

| File | Origin | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| %LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\protocol.js | vendor/protocol.js | pipe name, state set, redaction, snapshot |
| %LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe | vendor/AI-Terminal-Pet.exe | the Win32 overlay |

Nothing is ever overwritten: an existing file, including one placed by the
standalone installer, wins. Set DSH_PET_NO_BOOTSTRAP=1 to skip this step
entirely (for example when the overlay is managed by `scripts/install.ps1` already).

Reports also write the overlay's normal runtime snapshot under the same
directory, exactly like every other reporter.

### Optional download fallback

lib/release-pins.json is absent from the published package by default. When the
maintainer fills it in with pinned release asset URLs, sizes and SHA-256
digests, a machine that has no vendored binary downloads the two assets over
HTTPS with a 30 s timeout, verifies size and digest with node:crypto, and only
then installs them. Any failure is silent apart from one warning; the plugin
keeps working without an overlay.

## The overlay itself is still standalone

This bundle is a convenience. The overlay is a Go application that installs
normally with `scripts/install.ps1` from the repository, and every other reporter
(Claude Code, OpenCode, Antigravity, generic) talks to the same named pipe. A
machine that only wants the overlay does not need this package; a machine that
only wants the plugin gets one installed automatically.

## Requirements and limits

- Windows only (named pipes plus a Win32 layered window).
- Node 22.19+ or 24+ in the Harness runtime.
- Nothing in this package can fail the host: every entry point is wrapped,
  every report is fire-and-forget, and there is no process.exit.
- Session id is the Harness session.header.id; pid is a synthetic per-session
  id and parentPid is the real Harness process, which is how the overlay ties a
  session to its terminal window.

## English

### The problem

You run Claude Code, OpenCode, or Antigravity in multiple terminal windows at once. A background task prompts for permission to execute a tool, but you are focused in another window and never notice the prompt.

Fourteen minutes later, you switch back only to discover that your build has been sitting idle the entire time. Glancing across multiple terminal tabs wastes focus and breaks your concentration.

ai-terminal-pet anchors a 56px strip to the screen edge. It aggregates your sessions in real time, pulses when an agent needs permission, and displays which project is waiting and for how long.

The table below contrasts the everyday workflow before and after using the overlay:

| Context | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Multiple terminals | Four terminal windows open; you lose track of which window needs attention. | One 56px strip on the edge of the screen aggregates every active session. |
| Blocked build | You find out a build was blocked on a permission prompt fourteen minutes ago. | The overlay pulses immediately and shows which project is waiting and for how long. |
| Context switching | You click across tabs to check whether builds and tasks are still running. | A single glance reveals current states without touching your keyboard or mouse. |
